items.prompt: Which hook adds a piece of local state to a function component?

options.label: useMemo
useEffect
useState
useRef

rubric: useState declares state and returns the value plus a setter.
useEffect handles side effects, useRef holds mutable values, useMemo caches computed values.

items.prompt: What does `useState(0)` return?

options.label: A promise that resolves to the current state value
An object with `value` and `setValue` properties
Only the current state value, which is then changed directly
An array with the current state and a function to update it

rubric: useState returns a two-item array: state and setter.
The object-return distractor confuses it with other APIs.

items.prompt: What is the name of the second argument to `useEffect` that controls when the effect re-runs?

options.label: The initial state
The render callback
The cleanup function
The dependency array

rubric: The second argument is the dependency array.
The cleanup function is returned from the effect, not passed as an argument.

items.prompt: Which hook reads the current value of a React context?

options.label: useContext
useReducer
useLayoutEffect
useCallback

rubric: useContext reads the nearest provider's value.
The others serve state, memoization or effect timing.

items.prompt: By convention, what must the name of a custom hook start with?

options.label: hook
get
use
with

rubric: Custom hooks must start with 'use' so React and linters recognise them.
Other prefixes are not recognised by the rules of hooks.

items.prompt: Which of the following are built-in React hooks? Select all that apply.

options.label: useFetchData
useStore
useRef
useMemo

rubric: useRef and useMemo ship with React.
useStore and useFetchData are not built in; they would be library or custom hooks.

items.prompt: A teammate is writing a function component and wants to call `useState` to track a counter. They ask where in the component the call is allowed. Which rule of hooks answers this?

options.label: Call hooks only inside event handlers like onClick handlers
Call hooks inside any nested function that runs during render
Call hooks at the top level, never inside loops or conditions
Call hooks after the return statement once the JSX is built

rubric: Hooks must be called at the top level so their order is stable across renders.
Handlers, nested functions and conditions break the call order.

items.prompt: A component calls `setCount(count + 1)` in a click handler. What happens next?

options.label: React schedules a re-render with the new count value
The count variable changes immediately and no render occurs
The page reloads to show the new count value
The component is unmounted and mounted again from scratch

rubric: Calling a setter schedules a re-render with the new state.
State is not mutated in place, and the component is not remounted.

items.prompt: What does `useEffect(() => { document.title = name; }, [name])` do?

options.label: Updates the title whenever the document itself is changed
Updates the title once, only when the component first mounts
Updates the title after render, only when name has changed
Updates the title before every render, whatever changed

rubric: The dependency array limits the effect to renders where name changed.
An empty array would run only on mount; no array would run every render.

items.prompt: Why use `useRef` instead of `useState` to hold a DOM element reference?

options.label: State cannot store objects, so DOM nodes must go in refs
Refs are faster than state at storing large amounts of data
Refs are reset to null on every render, so they stay current
Changing ref.current does not trigger a re-render

rubric: Refs persist across renders and updating them doesn't re-render.
Refs are not reset each render, and state can hold objects.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the function returned from a `useEffect` callback?

options.label: It supplies the value that the component will render next
It runs first on mount to set up the effect's initial state, before the effect body runs
It cleans up, for example removing a listener, before the next run or unmount
It tells React to skip the effect on the next render

rubric: The returned function is cleanup, run before re-running and on unmount.
It does not provide render output or skip effects.

items.prompt: Why do two components that each call the same custom hook, such as `useCounter()`, not share their count?

options.label: The hook keeps its state in one global store keyed by the hook's name
Each call creates its own separate state inside its component
React locks the count to whichever component called the hook first
Custom hooks cannot hold state, since only built-in hooks can do that

rubric: Custom hooks share logic, not state; each call gets its own state.
They don't use a global store, and they can hold state via built-in hooks.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe `useEffect` with an empty dependency array `[]`? Select all that apply.

options.label: The effect runs after the first render
The effect runs after every single render
The effect runs before the component first renders
The effect does not re-run when props change

rubric: An empty array means run once after mount.
Running every render happens with no array; effects never run before the first render.

items.prompt: A component shows a theme color read with `useContext(ThemeContext)`. A parent provider's value changes from 'light' to 'dark'. What should a learner expect to happen to the component?

options.label: It ignores the change because context is read once
It re-renders and shows the new 'dark' value
It keeps showing 'light' until it is remounted
It throws an error since context values cannot change

rubric: Components using useContext re-render when the provider value changes.
Context is not read once, and its value may change.

items.prompt: What does calling `useState(0)` return inside a function component?

options.label: A getter function and a setter function for the state value
Only the current state value, which you reassign directly
An array holding the current state value and a function to update it
An object with a `state` property and a `dispatch` method for sending update actions

rubric: useState returns a two-item array: value and setter.
Distractors confuse it with useReducer, with plain variables, or with getter/setter pairs.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the dependency array in `useEffect(fn, [a, b])`?

options.label: It freezes `a` and `b` so the effect cannot update them
It lists the only props and state values the component may read during render
It sets the order in which several effects in one component will run
It makes React re-run the effect only when `a` or `b` changed

rubric: The array lets React skip the effect when listed values are unchanged.
Distractors treat it as a permissions list, an ordering tool, or a freeze on values.

items.prompt: A click handler calls `setCount(count + 1)` three times in a row, starting from `count = 0`. Why does count become 1 and not 3?

options.label: The setter ignores a new value when it is close to the old one
React drops every state update after the first one in a handler
Each call reads the same `count` of 0 from that render, so all set 1
Updates run after a timer, so the later calls get cancelled

rubric: The state value is a snapshot per render, so count + 1 is 1 each time.
Distractors invent dropping or cancelling of updates.

items.prompt: How does changing `ref.current` from `useRef` differ from calling a `useState` setter?

options.label: Changing the ref is lost on every render, but state persists
Changing the ref does not re-render, but a state update does
Changing the ref re-renders the component, but state does not
Both re-render, but the ref is only reset when unmounting

rubric: Refs persist across renders without triggering a render.
Distractors reverse the behaviour or claim refs reset each render.

items.prompt: Why must hooks be called in the same order on every render of a component?

options.label: Each hook needs a unique name that is based on its position
Hooks run faster when the engine sees a fixed order of calls
Conditional calls would be flagged as errors by the JavaScript engine
React matches each hook call to its stored state by call order

rubric: React tracks hooks by call order, so skipping one shifts the state.
Distractors give performance or language-engine reasons.

items.prompt: Which statements about the cleanup function returned from a `useEffect` callback are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: It runs once before the component's first render
It runs after every state update even when the dependencies are unchanged
It runs when the component unmounts
It runs before the effect re-runs after a dependency changes

rubric: Cleanup runs before the next effect run and on unmount.
Distractors place it before the first render or ignore the dependency array.

items.prompt: A `Profile` component receives a `userId` prop and loads the user in `useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId).then(setUser) }, [])`. When the parent changes `userId`, the old user stays on screen. What explains this?

options.label: `setUser` is ignored when it is called from inside a promise callback after render
The empty array means the effect only ran on mount, not for new `userId`
React keeps the first value of each prop and ignores later changes to `userId`
`fetchUser` must be called during render, because effects never run again after mount

rubric: With [] the effect runs only after the first render, so it misses new props.
Distractors blame promises, prop caching, or effects in general.

items.prompt: Starting at `count = 0`, which handler body makes `count` equal 3 after one click?

options.label: `setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(c => c + 1)`
`setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(count)`
`setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1)`
`setCount(count + 3); setCount(count)`

rubric: Functional updates chain on the latest pending state.
Other options reuse the stale count value of 0.

items.prompt: Given `useEffect(() => { document.title = `Clicks: ${n}` }, [n])`, `n` starts at 0 and the user clicks twice, so `n` goes 0, 1, 2. How many times does the effect run in total?
rubric: It runs on mount and after each change of n: 3 runs.
Choosing 2 forgets the mount run; 1 or 4 misread the dependency array.

items.prompt: Which implementation of a custom hook `useToggle` correctly returns `[on, toggle]`, where `toggle` flips the boolean?

options.label: `const [on, setOn] = useState(false); return [on, setOn(!on)]`
`const [on, setOn] = useState(false); return [on, () => setOn(o => !o)]`
`const [on, setOn] = useState(false); return [on, () => { on = !on; }]`
`const on = useRef(false); return [on, () => { on.current = !on.current; }]`

rubric: The toggle must be a function that calls the setter with the flipped value.
Other options call the setter during render or never update state.

items.prompt: A component calls `const theme = useContext(ThemeContext)` where `ThemeContext = createContext('light')`. It is rendered outside any `ThemeContext.Provider`. What is `theme`?

options.label: `'light'`, the default passed to `createContext`
`null`, because context is empty without a provider
`undefined`, because no provider supplies a value
It throws an error, because a provider is required

rubric: Without a provider, useContext returns the createContext default.
Distractors assume undefined, null, or an error.

items.prompt: A component has `useEffect(() => { setCount(count + 1) })` with no dependency array, and it re-renders endlessly. Which change makes the effect increment only once after mount?

options.label: Pass `[count]` as the dependency array to the effect
Wrap the call in `setTimeout(..., 0)` inside the effect
Pass `[]` as the dependency array to the effect
Replace `setCount` with a direct `count = count + 1`

rubric: An empty array limits the effect to the mount run.
[count] still loops because count changes each time.

items.prompt: Which of these usages break the rules of hooks? Select all that apply.

options.label: Calling `useEffect` inside a `for` loop body
Calling `useState` inside an `if` block in a component
Calling `useContext` inside a button's `onClick` handler
Calling `useRef` at the top level of a function component
Calling `useState` at the top level of a custom hook `useForm`

rubric: Hooks must not be called conditionally, in loops, or in handlers.
Top-level calls in components or custom hooks are allowed.

items.prompt: A form keeps `const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: '', age: '' })`. The name input uses `onChange={e => setForm({ name: e.target.value })}`. After typing a name, the age field's value disappears. Which change fixes it?

options.label: `setForm({ ...form, name: e.target.value })`
`setForm.name(e.target.value)`
`setForm({ name: e.target.value }, form.age)`
`setForm(form.name = e.target.value)`

rubric: The setter replaces state, so the other fields must be copied with spread.
Other options misuse the setter's signature or mutate state.

items.prompt: A component has `const [n, setN] = useState(0)`. A click handler runs `setN(n + 1); setN(n + 1); setN(n + 1);`. What is `n` after one click and the re-render?
rubric: All three calls use the same render's `n` (0), so each sets state to 1.
Choosing 3 assumes updates accumulate; a functional update `setN(c => c + 1)` would give 3.

items.prompt: Which effect fetches the user only when `userId` changes (and on mount)?

options.label: `useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId); }, [userId]);`
`useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId); }, []);`
`useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId); });`
`useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId); }, [fetchUser]);`

rubric: The dependency array lists `userId`, so the effect reruns only when it changes.
No array runs every render; an empty array runs once and ignores later ids.

items.prompt: An effect starts `const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);`. Which return statement correctly stops the timer on unmount?

options.label: `return () => setInterval(id, 0);`
`return () => { clearTimeout(tick); };`
`return () => clearInterval(id);`
`return clearInterval(id);`

rubric: An effect must return a cleanup function that calls `clearInterval`.
`return clearInterval(id)` runs immediately and returns undefined rather than a function.

items.prompt: A component does `const r = useRef(null);` and renders `<input ref={r} />`. After the first mount, what does `r.current` hold?

options.label: A copy of the component's latest state values
A function that returns the input's current value
The DOM input element, assigned after mount
The React element object created by the JSX

rubric: React assigns the DOM node to `ref.current` once mounted.
Confusing it with the JSX element or state misunderstands refs as handles to DOM nodes.

items.prompt: You must recompute `filter(items, query)` only when `items` or `query` changes. Which call does that?

options.label: `useMemo(() => filter(items, query), [items, query])`
`useMemo(() => filter(items, query), [items])`
`useMemo(filter(items, query), [items, query])`
`useMemo(() => filter(items, query), [items, query, filter])`

rubric: Every value the computation reads belongs in the dependency array.
Omitting `query` gives stale results; the last option calls filter immediately and passes its result, not a function.

items.prompt: State is `const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: 'Ana', age: 30 })`. Which updates correctly set age to 31 while keeping the name and triggering a re-render? Select all that apply.

options.label: `setUser({ age: 31 })`
`setUser(u => ({ ...u, age: 31 }))`
`user.age = 31; setUser(user);`
`setUser({ ...user, age: 31 })`

rubric: Spreading into a new object keeps name and creates a new reference.
Mutating then passing the same object is skipped by React; the last option drops `name`.

items.prompt: A theme context is created with `createContext('light')`. The app renders `<ThemeContext.Provider value="dark"><Header /></ThemeContext.Provider><Footer />`. Both Header and Footer call `useContext(ThemeContext)`. What does Footer receive?

options.label: `'dark'`
`undefined`
An error is thrown
`'light'`

rubric: Outside any provider, useContext returns the default value passed to createContext.
Assuming the nearest sibling's provider applies, or that it errors, misreads how providers scope.

items.prompt: A counter uses `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []);`. It shows 1 and never increases. What is the cause?

options.label: The interval callback closes over `count` from the first render, which is always 0
The empty array makes React skip state updates made from inside effects
Calling setCount inside an interval is batched and dropped until the next click
The cleanup function clears the interval after every tick, so only one update fires

rubric: A stale closure keeps `count` at 0, so it always sets 1; use `setCount(c => c + 1)`.
Cleanup runs only on unmount with an empty array; effects can set state freely.

items.prompt: A component has `const opts = { page: 1 };` in its body and `useEffect(() => { load(opts); }, [opts]);`. The effect runs after every render. Why?

options.label: Object dependencies are compared by key count and this one grows
`opts` is a new object each render, so its reference differs every time
`load` is called with an object, which React treats as a changed value
Effects always rerun when the dependency array has any object in it

rubric: Dependencies are compared with Object.is, and a fresh object literal has a new identity each render.
Fix by moving it outside, memoizing it, or depending on primitives like `page`.

items.prompt: A component starts with `if (!user) return null;` and then calls `useEffect(...)` below it. It works until `user` goes from set to null, then React errors. What is the fault?

options.label: Effects declared after a return statement are ignored on the first render
Hooks must run in the same order each render, and the early return skips one
useEffect cannot read props that may be null, so it throws when the effect callback runs
Returning null unmounts the component and discards its effect permanently, so it cannot re-render

rubric: The early return changes how many hooks are called between renders, breaking the rules of hooks.
Move the hook above the return and put the condition inside it.

items.prompt: A profile page fetches in `useEffect(..., [id])` and calls `setProfile(data)`. When users click through ids quickly, sometimes an older profile appears. What is the cause and fix?

options.label: Responses can arrive out of order; ignore stale ones with a flag set in cleanup
React caches the first fetch per component; remounting with a key avoids it
The dependency array is too narrow; adding `profile` to it orders the responses
setProfile is asynchronous; wrapping it in useMemo makes it apply in order

rubric: Earlier requests may resolve after later ones; cleanup can mark them ignored or abort them.
Adding state to dependencies or memoizing does not control response order.

items.prompt: `const onSave = useCallback(() => save(draft), [draft]);` is passed to a `React.memo` child, which still re-renders on every keystroke in a draft textbox. Why?

options.label: React.memo compares function props by value, and the new closure over the latest draft never matches
The child must also call useCallback itself before the parent's memoized callback is respected
useCallback only memoizes during the first render, so later memo comparisons see a new function
`draft` changes on each keystroke, so a new `onSave` function is created each time

rubric: The callback depends on `draft`, so its identity changes whenever the draft does.
Reading draft through a ref or restructuring would keep the callback stable.

items.prompt: An effect has the dependency array `[items]`. In which cases will it rerun on every render of the component? Select all that apply.

options.label: `const [items] = useState([]);` with no setter calls
`const items = data.filter(isActive);` in the component body
`const items = [1, 2, 3];` in the component body
`const items = useMemo(() => build(data), [data]);` with stable `data`

rubric: Body-level filter and array literals produce new references on every render.
State and memoized values keep the same reference until their inputs change.

items.prompt: A custom hook `useCounter()` wraps `useState(0)` and returns `[count, increment]`. A header and a sidebar both call it and the developer expects one shared count, but clicking in one never changes the other. What explains this?

options.label: The header renders first, so its state shadows the sidebar's state during updates
useState inside custom hooks resets whenever another component reads the value
Each call to a hook creates its own state, so the components hold separate counts
Custom hooks must be wrapped in useMemo to share their state between components

rubric: Hooks share logic, not state; every call gets independent state per component instance.
To share state, lift it up or put it in context; memoization does not merge instances.

items.prompt: A component runs `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []);` The counter moves to 1 and then stays there. What is the cause?

options.label: The callback closes over `count` from the first render, so every tick sets it to 1
React throttles state updates made from timers, so only the first update is ever applied
The empty dependency array makes the cleanup run before every tick, so the timer restarts
`setCount` is asynchronous, so ticks overwrite each other before React applies the updates

rubric: The effect runs once, so its closure keeps the first-render `count` (0) and always sets 1.
Distractors blame async setState or timer throttling, which misread how closures and dependencies work.

items.prompt: A component declares `const opts = { limit: 10 };` and runs `useEffect(() => { load(opts); }, [opts]);`. The effect fires after every render even though the values never change. Why?

options.label: `opts` is a new object on each render, and dependencies are compared by identity with `Object.is`
The `load` call sets state internally, and a state update always re-triggers every effect
Any dependency array containing a non-primitive value is treated by React as if it were missing
React compares object dependencies by key order, and the key order changes between renders

rubric: A fresh object literal has a new identity each render, so the shallow comparison reports a change.
Distractors invent key-order or deep-comparison rules that React does not use.

items.prompt: A search box runs an effect that calls `fetch(`/api?q=${q}`)` and then `setResults(data)` whenever `q` changes. Occasionally the list shows results for an older query than the one typed. What is the cause?

options.label: Responses can arrive out of order, and the effect has no cleanup to ignore a stale response
State setters called after an `await` are queued separately, so they apply in the wrong order
The effect runs before `q` updates, so it requests the previous query value each time
React batches the fetches and delivers their responses in reverse order of the requests

rubric: Without a cleanup flag or abort, a slow earlier request can resolve last and overwrite newer results.
Distractors suggest React reorders or delays requests, which it does not do.

items.prompt: `const Row = React.memo(RowImpl);` is rendered by a parent as `<Row onSelect={() => select(id)} />`. Profiling shows `Row` re-renders on every parent render. Why does `memo` not help?

options.label: The inline arrow is a new function each render, so the shallow prop check sees a change
React.memo compares props deeply, and functions with identical source text fail deep equality checks
React.memo is bypassed when a parent re-renders, unless the child also wraps its state in useMemo
React.memo skips renders for components that don't call hooks, and Row's hooks cause it to re-render

rubric: Memo does a shallow comparison, and a new function identity each render defeats it.
Distractors misstate memo's rules about hooks, deep comparison or forced child renders.

items.prompt: `App` renders `<Ctx.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>` and also re-renders often because of unrelated state. Components that read only `user` re-render each time, though `user` never changes. What explains this?

options.label: `useContext` subscribes to the whole provider tree, so any state change inside `App` notifies it
`setUser` is recreated each render, and context compares each field of the value separately
Consumers re-render whenever any ancestor re-renders, regardless of what the context value is
The value object is recreated every render, so consumers receive a new context value each time

rubric: A new object literal as the provider value changes identity, which triggers all consumers.
Distractors claim setters change identity or that context does per-field comparison; neither is true.

items.prompt: Which of these cause React to discard a component instance's hook state and start it fresh? Select all that apply.

options.label: The parent re-rendering and passing the component new prop values
Giving the component a different `key` than it had on the previous render
Rendering a different component type at the same position in the tree
Calling a state setter with a value equal to the current state

rubric: A changed key or changed element type at the same position unmounts the old instance and mounts a new one.
New props or an identical setter value never reset state.

items.prompt: A list component keeps `const [visible, setVisible] = useState([])` and runs `useEffect(() => { setVisible(items.filter(i => i.name.includes(query))); }, [items, query]);`. Users report that after typing, the list briefly shows old results for one frame before updating. What is the most accurate diagnosis?

options.label: `setVisible` is debounced by React, so the update applies several frames after the call
The filter is too slow to finish inside one render, so React paints the previous result
The dependency array is missing `visible`, so the effect works with a stale copy of it
The effect runs after the render is committed, so one painted frame uses stale derived state

rubric: Derived state set in an effect lags one committed render behind; computing it during render avoids that.
Distractors blame filter speed, debouncing or dependencies rather than effect timing.

items.prompt: A checkout form has six fields plus a status (idle, submitting, error). Many handlers update several fields together, and bugs come from inconsistent combinations. Criteria: make invalid combinations hard, centralise transitions, keep logic testable. Which approach is best?

options.label: A `useRef` holding all fields, because it avoids re-renders while the user types
`useReducer` with explicit actions, so every transition lives in one pure, testable function
One `useState` object spread in each handler, because it keeps all fields together in one place
Six separate `useState` calls, because each setter stays small and independent of the others

rubric: A reducer centralises coordinated transitions in one pure function that is easy to test.
Separate states or spread objects scatter the transition logic, and refs do not trigger renders.

items.prompt: Profiling shows an `items.reduce(...)` over 20 items takes 0.02 ms, and the component renders on every keystroke. A teammate proposes wrapping it in `useMemo`. Criteria: simplicity, correctness, real performance gain. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Wrap it in `useMemo`, because every computation inside a component body should be memoized by default
Leave it unmemoized, because dependency tracking and caching cost more than the tiny computation saves
Wrap it in `useMemo`, because that guarantees the result is never recomputed during the app's lifetime
Move it into `useEffect` with state, because effects run off the render path and cost nothing

rubric: Memoizing a trivial computation adds complexity and overhead without measurable benefit.
useMemo is a performance hint with no recompute guarantee, and moving derived values into effects adds renders.

items.prompt: One context holds `{ theme, cursor }`. The cursor updates 60 times per second, and 200 components read only `theme`. Criteria: minimal re-renders, little code change. Which design is best?

options.label: Wrap the single provider value in `useMemo` keyed on both fields, so consumers skip unrelated updates
Store both values in a `useRef` inside the provider, so consumers re-render only when they choose to
Split into `ThemeContext` and `CursorContext`, so theme readers never re-render on cursor updates
Keep one context and wrap the 200 consumers in `React.memo`, since memo blocks context-driven renders

rubric: Separate contexts isolate frequent updates from rarely changing values.
Memoizing a combined value still changes whenever cursor changes, and memo does not block context updates.

items.prompt: `ProfileForm` uses `useEffect(() => setDraft(''), [userId])` to clear its draft when the user changes, and a stale draft flashes for one render. Criteria: correctness, simplicity, no extra render. Which change is best?

options.label: Keep the effect but add `draft` to the dependency array, so the reset always sees the latest value
Render `<ProfileForm key={userId} />` so React remounts it with fresh state and no reset effect
Switch the effect to `useLayoutEffect`, since it runs synchronously and avoids any second render pass
Store the draft in `useRef` and reset it in the render body, since refs reset on prop change

rubric: A key change resets all state in the subtree without an extra render pass.
useLayoutEffect still renders twice, and refs do not reset on prop changes.

items.prompt: Fifteen components each combine `useEffect`, `fetch` and `useState` for loading and error. The team needs caching, deduping of identical requests, cancellation and consistent error handling. Which approach best meets all these needs?

options.label: Copy the effect into a shared `useFetch` custom hook, which adds caching by sharing the code
Add `AbortController` to each effect, because cancelling requests also provides caching and deduping
Adopt a hooks-based data-fetching library, so caching and deduping are handled once for all components
Lift every fetch into a root context provider, because shared state automatically dedupes requests

rubric: A dedicated library provides a shared cache and request deduping that hand-rolled hooks lack.
A shared hook only shares code, not cache; abort handles cancellation only.

items.prompt: A team writes `useEventListener(name, handler)`. Criteria: no missed events, no needless re-subscribing, no stale handler. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Use no dependency array so the listener is recreated every render with the latest handler
Omit `handler` from the dependencies and silence the lint rule, keeping the first handler
Return a cleanup that calls `removeEventListener` with the same function that was added
Store `handler` in a ref updated each render, and subscribe once per `name`
Subscribe inside the render body so no events are missed between render and effect

rubric: A ref gives the latest handler without re-subscribing, and cleanup must remove the exact listener added.
The other options keep a stale handler, cause side effects in render, or re-subscribe needlessly.

items.prompt: A tooltip measures its own height with `getBoundingClientRect` inside `useEffect` and then sets a `top` state. Users see it flash at the wrong position for one frame. Criteria: no visible flash, minimal blocking of paint. Which change is best?

options.label: Read the ref's size during render, since refs are populated before the first render finishes and the DOM node is ready
Keep `useEffect` but wrap `setTop` in `useMemo`, since memoized values are applied before paint
Delay showing the tooltip with `setTimeout` in `useEffect`, since a timer hides the flash at no cost
Measure and set the position in `useLayoutEffect`, since it runs before paint and the measure is cheap

rubric: useLayoutEffect runs after DOM updates but before paint, so measure-then-position produces no flash.
Refs are null during first render, useMemo does not schedule effects, and timers just hide the problem.

items.prompt: A search box calls `fetch` inside `useEffect` keyed on `query`. Slow responses sometimes arrive after newer ones and overwrite the results. Criteria: no stale overwrite, no wasted network work, minimal code. Which fix is best?

options.label: Remove `query` from the dependency array so that only one request is ever in flight at a time
Wrap the fetch call in `useMemo` keyed on `query` so older responses get discarded by React
Abort the request via an `AbortController` in the effect cleanup and ignore the `AbortError`
Add a 500ms `setTimeout` before each fetch so that responses finish in the order they were sent

rubric: Aborting in cleanup cancels superseded requests and prevents stale state writes.
Distractors assume memoization or delays control response order, or that an empty dependency list avoids races.

items.prompt: A provider renders `<Ctx.Provider value={{user, setUser}}>` and its parent re-renders often for unrelated reasons. Dozens of consumers re-render each time. Criteria: stop needless consumer renders, keep the consumer API unchanged. Which option is best?

options.label: Memoize the value with `useMemo` over `[user]`; `setUser` is stable, so identity changes only with `user`
Keep the value in a `useRef` so the provider never triggers any consumer update, even when `user` changes later on
Copy `user` into each consumer's own state with a `useEffect` so consumers no longer depend on the context at all
Wrap every consumer in `React.memo`, which blocks re-renders that are triggered by a changed context value from the provider

rubric: A new object each render changes context identity; memoizing it limits updates to real changes of `user`.
`React.memo` does not block context-driven updates, and refs or copied state lose needed updates or duplicate truth.

items.prompt: A checkout flow tracks `status`, `items` and `error`. Transitions are interdependent (for example, a failure must clear `items` loading and set `error` together). Criteria: impossible states are avoided and the logic is testable without rendering. Which approach fits best?

options.label: One `useEffect` per field that re-syncs it with the others whenever any of the other fields change
A mutable `useRef` object changed in handlers, so updates never have to wait for a render to finish
A `useReducer` with a pure reducer over named actions, so each transition sets all related fields together
Several `useState` calls that handlers update one after another, so that each field stays simple on its own

rubric: A pure reducer centralises transitions, prevents inconsistent combinations and can be unit-tested.
Separate setters and sync effects allow intermediate inconsistent states; refs skip re-rendering.

items.prompt: A teammate proposes wrapping every function in every component with `useCallback` "for performance". Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: It breaks the rules of hooks, because `useCallback` may only be called once in each component body
It is harmless, because memoized functions cost nothing and always let React skip work on later renders
It only pays off when identity matters, such as memoized children or effect dependencies; elsewhere it adds cost
It is required, because otherwise each recreated function causes React to rebuild the DOM nodes it touches

rubric: Memoizing helps only where referential equality is consumed; otherwise it adds comparison and dependency overhead.
Distractors claim it is free, mandatory for DOM efficiency, or forbidden by the rules of hooks.

items.prompt: A tooltip measures its own height via a ref to position itself above its anchor. With `useEffect` it flashes at the wrong place for one frame. Criteria: no visible flicker, and the trade-off is acknowledged. Which hook is the best choice?

options.label: `useLayoutEffect`, because it runs after DOM updates but before paint, at the cost of blocking paint
`useMemo` reading `ref.current.offsetHeight`, since memo callbacks run after the DOM has been committed
`useEffect` with an empty dependency array, since it always runs earlier than any layout effect would
`useInsertionEffect`, because it is the hook intended for measuring DOM nodes and positioning elements

rubric: Layout effects run synchronously before paint so measured updates avoid flicker, but they delay painting.
`useEffect` runs after paint; `useMemo` runs during render before refs are set; `useInsertionEffect` is for style injection.

items.prompt: A component copies a prop into state with `useEffect(() => setLocal(props.value), [props.value])` and renders `local`. Which are valid criticisms of this pattern? Select all that apply.

options.label: Effects cannot read props, so `props.value` is always the initial value inside the effect callback
It creates two sources of truth for one value, which can drift apart when `local` is also edited elsewhere
If `local` is only a transformation of the prop, computing it during render avoids the extra render pass
A `setLocal` call inside an effect always causes an infinite render loop, whatever the dependency list is
Each prop change renders once with the stale `local` before the effect runs, so users can see an out-of-date frame

rubric: Effect-synced state adds a stale render and a duplicate source of truth; derived values belong in render.
Effects do read current props, and a dependency list prevents an infinite loop here.

items.prompt: A `useWindowSize` hook returns `{width, height}` from a resize listener. Forty components use it only to check `width < 768`, and profiling shows them re-rendering on every pixel of a resize. Criteria: re-render only when the breakpoint flips, and use a subscription that is safe under concurrent rendering. Which change is best?

options.label: Subscribe with `useSyncExternalStore` to a `matchMedia('(max-width: 767px)')` snapshot that returns a boolean
Throttle the resize handler to 16ms so that state still updates about sixty times per second
Wrap each of the forty components in `React.memo` so they skip updates even though hook state changes
Store the width in a `useRef` and read it during render so that no component is notified of changes

rubric: A boolean snapshot from an external store only triggers renders when the value changes and is tear-free.
Throttling still renders often; refs never notify; `React.memo` cannot stop a component's own hook state from re-rendering it.

items.prompt: Design `useEventListener(target, name, handler)`. Constraints: subscribe once per `target` and `name`, never call a stale `handler` even though it closes over changing state. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Wrap `handler` in `useMemo` with an empty array so the listener always receives its newest version
Capture `handler` in the subscribing effect with an empty dependency array so the first closure gets reused
Store `handler` in a ref updated each render, and subscribe once with a listener that calls `ref.current`
Put `handler` in a dependency array and resubscribe on each change, treating resubscription as cheap and correct

rubric: A ref holding the latest handler plus a stable listener satisfies both once-only subscription and freshness.
Resubscribing violates the once constraint, and empty-array capture or memo freezes the first closure.

items.prompt: A counter uses `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])` and sticks at 1. Constraints: the interval is created once, the count rises every second, and no extra refs are used. Which fix meets all of them?

options.label: Change `[]` to `[count]` so the interval is recreated whenever the count changes
Move `count` into a `useRef` and read `count.current + 1` inside the callback each tick
Call `setCount(count + 1)` twice per tick so that one of the calls sees the updated value
Change the callback to `setCount(c => c + 1)` and keep the empty dependency array

rubric: A functional update reads the latest state, so the single interval needs no fresh closure.
Other options recreate the interval, still use the stale closure, or add the ref the constraints exclude.

items.prompt: Design `useDebouncedValue(value, delay)`. Constraints: it returns the latest value only after `delay` ms without changes, leaves no timer running after unmount, and reacts correctly if `delay` changes. Which implementation fits?

options.label: `useState` plus a `useEffect` that sets a `setTimeout` and returns `clearTimeout`, depending on `[value, delay]`
A `useRef` holding the value, changed by a `setTimeout` that is started in the render body on each render
`useMemo(() => value, [])` wrapped in a `setTimeout` so the value updates only after the delay passes
A `useEffect` with `setTimeout`, no cleanup, and `[]` dependencies so only the first timer is ever created

rubric: Effect cleanup cancels pending timers on change and unmount; both inputs are dependencies.
Other options skip cleanup, ignore dependencies, or start side effects during render.

items.prompt: A reducer-based provider must satisfy: components that only call `dispatch` never re-render when state changes, there is one provider component, and `dispatch` is stable. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Two contexts from one provider: the state in one context and the stable `dispatch` in the other
One context carrying `state`, with `dispatch` imported from a module variable assigned during render
One context carrying `{state, dispatch}` in `useMemo`, since consumers re-render only when memo dependencies change
One context whose value is a ref to the state, with consumers calling a forced update on every dispatch

rubric: Separating state and dispatch contexts lets dispatch-only consumers avoid state updates.
A combined value changes whenever state does; the other options are fragile or defeat the goal.

items.prompt: Design `useChatRoom(roomId)`. Constraints: connect to the room, switch cleanly when `roomId` changes, and behave correctly when StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts effects in development. Which design fits?

options.label: Connect in the component body behind `if (!connection)` so that rendering twice opens only one connection and the room is reused
Connect in an effect with `[]` dependencies and disconnect only in a `beforeunload` listener, so room changes cause no reconnect churn
Connect in an effect and guard it with a `useRef` flag so the second development invocation is skipped and only one connection opens
Connect in an effect keyed on `[roomId]` that returns a cleanup which disconnects, so remounting ends with one connection

rubric: A symmetric setup and cleanup keyed on `roomId` is correct under re-invocation and room changes.
Flags, render-time connections and page-level cleanup hide bugs and leak connections on room change.

items.prompt: Design `useLocalStorage(key, initial)`. Constraints: safe to render on a server, values sync across browser tabs, rapid updates compose correctly. Which elements does a design need? Select all that apply.

options.label: Guard with `typeof window` or provide a server snapshot so server rendering never touches `localStorage`
Read `localStorage` in the component body on every render with no subscription, since reading is always fresh
Write `useState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key)))` so parsing reruns on each render for correctness
Accept functional updates in the setter and compute from the latest stored value before writing it
Subscribe to the `storage` event and return an unsubscribe cleanup, so other tabs' writes reach the hook

rubric: Tab sync needs a storage subscription, server safety needs a guard, and composed updates need functional setters.
Unsubscribed reads never notify of changes, and the eager initializer runs each render and breaks on the server.

items.prompt: A `ProfileEditor` holds a dozen `useState` fields. When the route's `userId` changes, the previous user's draft flashes and sometimes persists. Constraints: all local state resets on a change, no frame shows old data, and no effect is used to sync state. Which fix meets every constraint?

options.label: Add a `useEffect` on `[userId]` that calls every setter with defaults, resetting after the next paint
Wrap the editor in `React.memo` with a comparator on `userId` so it re-renders just for new users
Store each field in a `useRef` so a changed `userId` does not leave stale drafts inside state
Render `<ProfileEditor key={userId} />` so React remounts it with fresh state for each user

rubric: Changing `key` remounts the component, resetting all state before any stale frame is shown.
Reset effects run after paint, refs retain values, and memo comparators do not reset state.
